article.title: ‘Why has the Chancellor left the wealthiest untouched?’ – our money and economics writers answered your questions

article.content: The Guardian’s money and economics editors Hilary Osborne and Heather Stewart answered your questions on energy prices, tax thresholds and the global events pressuring the economy. FelonMarmer asks : What is going to stop landlords just transferring their tax increase onto tenants, while complaining about how hard done by they are? Heather says : Unfortunately, there’s nothing to stop landlords passing their higher tax bills onto their tenants, aside from what the local rental market will bear. Indeed, the Office for Budget Responsibility did suggest one result of this and other recent policies (the 2p rise this year followed another 2p last year) could be “a steady rise in rents,” as some landlords whack up rents and others leave the market altogether. I think John Healey’s answer would probably be a fairness one - that income made through renting out property should be taxed more heavily than that earned through work. Heather says: That’s a really good question: Labour strategists are adamant that they wouldn’t. I can’t help thinking that voters were so convinced the public services were in a dire state, they could have accepted the argument that taxes needed to rise. Certainly, the Tories didn’t seem to get much electoral credit for Jeremy Hunt’s desperate cuts to national insurance contributions in his last couple of budgets. But we’ll never know. Another question is whether Labour should have bust the manifesto promises - either when they first got in, on the basis the public finances were worse than they thought; or at some point in the last year, given the impact of the Iran war (which has added £14bn to the government’s interest costs this year alone). Readers seeking clarity on recent financial shifts turned directly to financial journalists on **October 29, 2026**, according to **Business | The Guardian**. In a live question-and-answer session hosted by the publication, money and economics editors **Hilary Osborne** and **Heather Stewart** addressed public concerns regarding national economic pressures. The interactive forum focused heavily on how macroeconomic trends, energy costs, and fiscal policy directly impact household finances across the country. 

As financial pressures mount, citizens frequently look to specialized reporters to decode complex policy decisions and global market fluctuations. For instance, sports enthusiasts following massive financial investments in athletics might also reflect on broader economic realities, much like the elite-level shifts seen when an athlete achieves an [amazing achievement as Rybakina clinches year-end number one ranking](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/amazing-achievement-as-rybakina-clinches-year-end-number-one-ranking). Public anxiety remains high as everyday consumers try to reconcile official fiscal policy with their rising monthly expenses.

## Addressing Tax Thresholds and Landlord Policies

According to the report from **Business | The Guardian**, readers submitted pressing inquiries about structural economic changes, including how landlords might respond to shifting tax regulations. A participant identified as **FelonMarmer** specifically questioned what measures would prevent property owners from simply passing tax burdens directly onto tenants. While the published excerpt outlined this specific tenant concern regarding housing affordability, the journalists' detailed replies formed part of a broader dialogue on wealth distribution. Another prominent reader question challenged why the Chancellor allegedly left the wealthiest demographics untouched by recent fiscal adjustments.

Economic policy discussions regularly spark intense public debate over fairness, housing stability, and the distribution of tax responsibilities between renters and property owners. Similar intense public interest and scrutiny of authority figures can be observed across various cultural domains, such as when public figures or young talents face immense pressure, echoing how [a three-year-old soccer prodigy went viral. The adults have already let him down](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/a-three-year-old-soccer-prodigy-went-viral-the-adults-have-already). 

## Analyzing the Economic Stakes

> **Context:** The ongoing debate over tax thresholds and energy prices highlights a deep national anxiety surrounding the cost of living and housing security. When fiscal policies fail to address perceived inequalities, working-class households bear the brunt of inflation and operational costs. For policymakers, balancing state revenue needs with public demands for fairness remains a delicate tightrope walk, particularly as global supply chains and geopolitical events continue to squeeze national markets. Observers should monitor upcoming legislative debates and Treasury announcements for any signs of retroactive adjustments to landlord taxation or wealth levies as public pressure mounts.
